title: A dictionary is a data structure that uses keys to look up values.
body: A `dict` is a data structure that stores keys and values as pairs. Since this card serves as the foundational card for defining dictionaries, it establishes the structure itself before other review cards do.
detail: While a list looks up values by their positions (such as 0 or 1), a `dict` looks up values using keys, which act like labels. For example, in `user = {'name': 'Mina', 'age': 13}`, `user['name']` is an expression that retrieves 'Mina'. Here, 'name' is the name being searched for, and 'Mina' is the value associated with that name.

title: `get` can safely handle keys that don't exist
body: get returns None or a chosen default when a key is absent. This suits optional fields, but it can hide invalid input when the key is required.
detail: Use bracket access or explicit validation for required fields, and confirm that the default is meaningful in the domain.

title: "keys," "values," and "items" are three ways of looking at a dictionary.
when_to_show: When checking the keys, values, and pairs in a dictionary
body: Use `dict.keys()` to view the keys, `dict.values()` to view the values, and `dict.items()` to view key-value pairs.
detail: For example, if you only need the names from a score dictionary, use `keys`; if you only need the scores, use `values`; and if you want to print both names and scores together, `items` is the appropriate choice. Items are frequently used in loops, as in `for name, score in scores.items()`. When reading code, you must distinguish what exactly is being iterated over.

title: You can add or change values in a dictionary.
when_to_show: When adding a new key to a dictionary or changing an existing value
body: You can use keys to add or change values in a dictionary.
detail: If you assign a value to an existing key—such as `user['age'] = 14`—the value is updated; if you assign a value to a key that doesn’t exist—such as `user['city'] = 'Seoul'`—a new entry is added. When reading code, you should distinguish between the state of the dict before and after an assignment. It’s also important to note that if you assign a value to the same key multiple times, only the last value remains.

title: A tuple is an ordered collection whose elements are typically not modified.
when_to_show: When returning a value enclosed in parentheses or multiple values at once
body: A tuple is ordered and its slots cannot be reassigned. A tuple can still contain a mutable list or dictionary whose contents change.
detail: Track both the positional meaning of returned values and the mutability of nested objects.

title: Unpacking splits a bound value among multiple variables.
when_to_show: When reading code like `a, b = pair`,
body: Unpacking is a method of breaking down a group of values—such as a tuple or list—into multiple variables. For example, if you write `point = (3, 4)` and then `x, y = point`, `x` becomes 3 and `y` becomes 4.
detail: When iterating over `dict.items()`, receiving the key and value separately—as in `for key, value in data.items()`—is also related to unpacking. When reading code, you must verify that the number of variables on the left matches the number of values on the right. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how data structures store and retrieve values in actual Python code.

title: A set is a collection of unique values.
when_to_show: When checking for duplicates or determining whether to include an item
body: A set is a collection of values that does not allow duplicates. Even if a list contains the same value multiple times, converting it to a set will leave only one instance.
detail: For example, `set(['a', 'a', 'b'])` can be thought of as `{'a', 'b'}`. Sets are useful when the presence or absence of a value is more important than its order. When reading code, you should check whether a set is being used to reduce the number of elements, to remove duplicates, or to quickly verify if a value is present.

title: Set operations are used to find similarities and differences.
when_to_show: When finding the common value or the combined value of two sets
body: Sets are useful for examining the relationships between two sets of values. You can use `a | b` for the union, `a & b` for the intersection, and `a - b` for the difference.
detail: For example, by comparing the set of concepts you’ve already learned with the set of concepts you mastered today, you can identify common concepts or areas where you still need improvement. When reading code, you must verify that the symbols represent relationships between sets rather than calculations. This card is not intended merely for memorizing word definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how data structures store and retrieve values in actual Python code.
